source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 8 (Soil and nutrient management for rice), by Seng Vang, Phal Sovuthy, Hun Sarik, Tuor Chantha and Touch Vathna, section 8.1.1 (Geomorphology and geology). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Cambodia's rice-growing soils are classified in this source by how they formed (parent material and landscape position), which helps explain why soil fertility and management needs vary by location even within the same general region. Parent material categories named: old alluvial deposits (ដីទំនាបល្បាប់ចាស់, soils formed from old river/lake sediment, common in lowland rice areas), colluvium (soil formed from material washed down from higher ground), residual/weathered parent rock (soil formed in place from underlying rock), and marine floodplain alluvial deposits (ដីវិវឌ្ឍនៅលើវាលទំនាបលិចទឹក, soils influenced by past marine/estuarine conditions). Floodplains themselves are further classified into types: expansive floodplains (វាលទំនាបលិចទឹកធំ, broad flat flood-prone areas), meander floodplains (associated with a river's meandering path and point-bar deposits), marine floodplains (near coastal/estuarine influence), and lacustrine floodplains (associated with lake systems, e.g. around the Tonle Sap). Soil properties - particularly topsoil texture and fertility - are strongly influenced by which of these geomorphological categories a given field falls into, which is why the same fertilizer or water-management recommendation does not always translate well from one landscape position to another.
caveat: This is background soil-science classification content (citing Saeki et al., 1959; Crocker, 1962; Kawaguchi and Kyuma, 1974) rather than a specific fertilizer recommendation - useful context for the soil-type-and-NPK-rate content already in this knowledge base from earlier batches (the 11 CARDI national soil groups). Recommend a duplicate-check to see whether this geomorphology-based framework is the same system, complementary to, or distinct from the existing 11-soil-group content, since this project has an open item (from Batch 13) about reconciling different soil-group-count systems.
